items.title: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
items.summary: China's immense clout now also has the flex of soft power. Critics and dissidents say their voices are being drowned out.
items.content:
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.

"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."

It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.

But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.

It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .

But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".

Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls , Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.

China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power , drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.

Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.

Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.

The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.

China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.

"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."

China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.

This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.

In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.

His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.

That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.

"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.

Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".

The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? "We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."

Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.

"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.

These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.

In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.

"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.

Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.

The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.

"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.

Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.

Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.

"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim.

"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political."

When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.

The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".

"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.

"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable."

These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.

Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips.

"Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he says. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety."

The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen.

"They get sidelined when they return... Very sadly, our suspicions that some of them are feeding information back to the Chinese authorities have turned out to be true."

Rinchen serves as information secretary in the Tibetan government-in-exile in the northern Indian town of Dharamshala. His parents were among thousands who followed their spiritual leader Dalai Lama into exile after China annexed Tibet.

Over the decades, waves of others have fled Chinese rule seeking greater freedom or asylum from Beijing's crackdowns - dissidents and student activists in the wake of the Tiannanmen Square massacre; lawyers, journalists, purged officials and critics in the years after, and, more recently, Hong Kong saw a steady exodus build as the pro-democracy movement was crushed.

Many have kept on fighting. But now, they say, Beijing's might is chipping away at their struggle, making it ever harder to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party.

"Many among us have been separated from our families for generations and are eager to set foot on Tibet soil," Rinchen says. "This is exactly the kind of desperation the Communist Party seeks to target."

items.title: Perché a volte il tennis vale doppio
items.summary: La rubrica “Monday’s net"
items.content:
Novembre 2022-novembre 2026, quattro anni, cinque edizioni della Davis, tre titoli vinti (due con Jannik Sinner, uno senza), forse un quarto trionfo tra due giorni, cinque semifinali: abbiamo o no la nazionale più forte del mondo? O, se non la più forte, di sicuro la più costante nei risultati.

I campioni in carica erano dati per sfavoriti nella semifinale di Bologna, che è una condizione che di solito non porta male. Capita anche oggi, l'underdog non cede il passo nemmeno alla Repubblica Ceca (o Cechia, se preferite) di capitan Tomas Berdych, ex numero 4 del mondo, che non è lo squadrone che spadroneggiò nel biennio 2012-2013 ma dispone di due ottimi singolaristi tra i Top 15 ATP e di una discreta coppia di doppio. Giustamente, i bookmaker quotavano il suo passaggio in finale fra 1,73 e 1,75, quello italiano fra 2,00 e 2,05.

Brevi cronache dalla nuova arena della Fiera. Lorenzo Musetti apre le danze nel pomeriggio, Flavio Cobolli segue contro Jiri Lehecka. Berdych rischia subito la carta Jakub Mensik, tenuto fuori martedì contro il Canada per i postumi di un guaio fisico. Il carrarino numero 27 ATP, rotto il ghiaccio due giorni fa nel match contro il coreano Seongchan Hong, fa il capolavoro contro il ceco numero 15 ATP. Efficace al servizio, quand'è alla risposta riesce più volte a recuperare lo svantaggio contro uno dei migliori “serve men” del circuito (13 ace oggi, peraltro annullati da 25 errori con il diritto). In entrambi i set si procura i break quando fanno più male, nell'ottavo e nel settimo gioco, e poi li difende fino a prendersi il match per 6-3 6-4 in meno di un'ora e mezza.

Flavio le prova di ogni risma per seguire le tracce di Lollo. Tutto va per il giusto verso in un unico set, il secondo. Negli altri due subisce il gioco geometrico e potente di Lehecka, che nel ranking ATP in tempo reale è piazzato subito prima di Mensik. Il romano lotta allo stremo per recuperare un break disgraziato nel quarto game del terzo parziale e fa spellare le mani al pubblico: niente da fare, finisce 6-2 1-6 6-3 in un'ora e 40 minuti.

Come mercoledì, toccherebbe alla coppia azzurra titolare tentare di rimediare battendo gli specialisti Adam Pavlasek e Patrik Rikl e timbrare il pass per la finale. Invece i due capitani sparigliano: Filippo Volandri ha già deciso che Matteo Berrettini, che ha un dolore al braccio, debba cedere il posto a Musetti; Berdych schiera a sorpresa Lehecka e Tomas Machac. In campo, l'unico doppista a tempo pieno resta Andrea “Wave” Vavassori.

Strategie al minimo, le coppie limitano all'essenziale i tipici segnali prima di ogni servizio. Gli scambi sono fulminei, i set velocissimi, i primi due restano sotto la mezz'ora ciascuno, uno va ai cechi (3-6), l'altro agli azzurri (6-1).Il terzo parziale è il più equilibrato, si va di conserva per dodici giochi, che non significa affatto che lo spettacolo sia carente, anzi: servizi a oltre duecento all'ora, scambi finalmente prolungati, pezzi di bravura sia da fondo campo, sia sotto rete. Il tie-break è più breve ma altrettanto emozionante di quello di 48 ore prima, Andrea e Lorenzo sono costretti a inseguire ma alla fine prevalgono per 7-4. Si va a domenica, domani sapremo se contro i britannici o gli spagnoli.

“Numerantur enim sententiae, non ponderantur”, scriveva Plinio il Giovane diciannove secoli fa: i voti si contano, non si pesano. Non era un elogio della democrazia, era il lamento di un senatore costretto a vedere il parere di uno sciocco valere quanto quello di un saggio. Il tennis non gli avrebbe dato soddisfazione, perché è uno dei pochi sport nei quali si possono fare più punti dell'avversario e uscire battuti senza che nessuno gridi allo scandalo. Oggi Musetti ha vinto mettendo a segno 63 quindici contro i 53 di Mensik. Ma lo sconfitto Cobolli ne ha accumulati 68 contro i 67 di Lehecka. Lollo e Wave 22 più degli avversari (89 a 67). Mercoledì Cobolli aveva messo insieme 126 punti contro i 122 di Soonwoo Kwon, numero 139 del mondo, e tuttavia aveva perso. Il tabellone ha sempre l'ultima parola.

Non è una stranezza da Davis. Nel giugno 2024, davanti ai laureati di Dartmouth, Roger Federer ricordò di aver vinto quasi l'80 per cento delle sue 1526 partite di singolare aggiudicandosi appena il 54 per cento dei punti. Il più elegante dei dominatori ne perdeva quasi uno su due. E nella finale di Wimbledon 2019 ne fece 218 contro i 204 di Novak Djokovic: il trofeo lo alzò il serbo.

La morale è che al massimo livello il margine non esiste, esiste il momento. Si gioca per ore attorno alla parità e poi qualcuno mette una prima sulla riga quando conta. Oppure.come Musetti stasera, approfitta di una palla facile facile per uno smash che fa saltare tutti dalle sedie: per farci godere un'altra giornata di (piccola) gloria azzurra.

items.title: Prosecutors seek 25-year prison term for 'poison seller' Kenneth Law
items.summary: The Canadian man, who pleaded guilty to 14 counts of aiding and abetting suicide earlier this year, will be sentenced at a later date.
items.content:
Canadian prosecutors are seeking a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries.

Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.

The 61-year-old will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.

During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.

If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.

As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".

"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.

"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.

Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for many of their battles with mental illness.

He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims.

"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."

Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.

The sentencing hearing on Friday followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.

Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.

Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.

If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

items.title: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
items.summary: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez wants to defy the polls, and his main rivals accuse him of not telling the truth and of "betrayal".
items.content:
Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.

"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.

Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".

He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.

The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.

Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.

"This time, yes, we're going to do it," Feijóo told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.

If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in front of thousands of people in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.

The venue was filled with Spanish flags and green Vox banners, and one of the biggest cheers of the night came when the secretary general of the party called for "less burka and less halal".

Ignacio Garriga said he was not acting out of hatred but love for the homeland.

A small section of the crowd could be heard chanting "Viva Franco" in reference to the dictator, whose death in 1975 heralded the start of Spain's transition to democracy.

A number of first-time voters at the rally said they were supporting Vox because of its policies on immigration.

Lledó, 18, said what had happened in Ceuta in the summer, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory from Morocco, showed Sánchez was not able to control the country's border.

She had come to the bullring with her mum and aunt, Carli Chilet, who argued that Vox "are the best for women's rights".

Vox is hoping to almost double its seats from the 33 it won three years ago. It backs policies such as "national priority" - putting Spanish citizens first for welfare - and "remigration" for foreigners not considered to be contributing to the economy.

Leaders clash in final Spain election debate as housing dominates run-in

Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election

The final day of campaigning was very much in the shadow of a four-way TV debate the night before that exposed Spain's sharply polarised politics.

All four leaders had solutions for the housing crisis. Feijóo said the PP would build a million homes over four years, while Sánchez said housing should be a right not an object of speculation and profit.

While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.

The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.

Sánchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism.

Feijóo sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.

Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, Aragón, and Castilla y León.

Feijóo has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power.

"Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," he said in Seville.

One of his new supporters at the rally was a retired woman called Isabel who told Spanish public broadvaster RTVE that she was attending a PP rally for the first time. The formerly loyal Socialist voter said she was "disillusioned" with a party led by Sánchez. Another voter at the rally said Spain needed "a good manager".

Sánchez took to the stage in Madrid with his wife Begoña Gómez, and donned a red T-shirt that read "power of the people".

He then went on to praise Colau and her left-wing coalition's campaign.

"These elections are about moving Spain forward, not taking it backwards," he said.

Socialist supporter Leon Felipe, 25, told Reuters news agency: "Well, I think what's at stake in these elections is a big deal, is not a change of government... but rather a return to the past - a return to Franco's dictatorship.

As he was speaking, Colau told a large audience in the south of Madrid that not only would they "not remain silent, we will win", vowing to form another "progressive government".

items.title: Capsized tanker carrying 7,000 tonnes of diesel to be towed away from Ibiza
items.summary: There are fears of a major oil spillage off Ibiza but the ship's fuel tanks are so far intact.
items.content:
A tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel which capsized off the holiday island of Ibiza on Thursday will be towed to the port of Cartagena, officials in Spain say.

All 17 of the Malta-registered Med Emre's crew members were rescued but the chief engineer later died in hospital. Six people were treated for minor injuries.

There had been concerns of a major oil spillage in the western Mediterranean but an inspection showed that the ship's fuel tanks are intact. An investigation is under way into what happened.

The vessel had been travelling from Algeciras near Gibraltar to Barcelona and is expected to arrive in Cartagena on Monday in what is being seen as a challenging rescue operation.

In a statement on Friday, the Spanish transport ministry said the tanker would be towed to Cartagena "as it is the only one [port] that meets the technical requirements to carry out cargo extraction and repair work".

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told Cadena SER radio network he hoped the tanker could be taken to port "in the coming hours, in the coming days".

"The information suggests that, indeed... this leak is not happening", he added.

The Spanish authorities provided no details about how the diesel would be extracted.

Meanwhile, pictures have emerged showing emergency workers inspecting the tanker's hull.

Any possible environmental damage is being assessed by air and pollution control vessel Clara Campoamor, which is owned by Spain's national maritime rescue service.

Elena Delgado, maritime captain of the port of Valencia, earlier told news agency AFP that a small slick which had formed around the vessel had "disappeared".

"The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out.

Regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk as originally reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.

The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia.

Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call late on Wednesday, according to Spanish media.

Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle. It capsized in the early hours on Thursday.

Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.

In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline, in the country's north-west.

More than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil spilled into the sea.

items.title: 'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
items.summary: Stormy weather in New York City prompted organisers to push back the Macy's parade by two days - leaving some musicians stuck.
items.content:
Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.

"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.

Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (£267,000) in just a few hours.

Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.

On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.

The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.

The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.

Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.

Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving

Demkovich described an emotional and exhausting experience, first learning that the parade would be postponed while watching a Broadway performance of Wicked with his band.

"My initial thought was like, 'Oh, crap. We're not going to be able to go'," he said.

"Where are we going to be able to get all the money for this?"

The delay meant unexpected expenses of additional nights in a hotel - and meals - for hundreds of people in the middle of New York City during the holidays.

There were no vacancies to extend their stay at the New York Marriott Marquis in Times Square, so they booked the nearest hotel with availability - across the Hudson River - in New Jersey.

Demkovich said the Pride of Pearland Marching Band posted a fundraiser online and within hours met its fundraising goal.

"The word just spread like wildfire, truly like wildfire," Demkovich said, adding that donations came from over 2,000 people and local businesses.

He called the outpouring of support "very, very overwhelming to think about and comprehend".

Some groups were not able to maneuver as easily. The University of Alabama's Million Dollar Band is one of those missing out, due to a schedule conflict on Saturday.

“‘This can’t be happening’,” Rina Browder, mother of a snare drummer in the band, told local news, describing the band’s reactions.

"They were devastated. They've worked so hard for this. So many practices."

Meanwhile, a group from Hawaii, the Nā Koa Aliʻi Hawaiʻi All-State Marching Band, said it too would still be able to participate in the parade, also because of emergency fundraising by families, friends and other supporters donating more than $500,000.

Speaking to the BBC on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained.

The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to New York.

"Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional for our students," Badua said.

But the musicians sprang into action quickly, he said. "We come from a very far place," Badua said, adding that "to get so close to the finish line and not show up for it, we couldn't give up that easily".

The response from friends and family had been "incredible", he said.

Badua was hopeful his group would have the same experience he had when he first performed at the parade in 2003, as student drum major.

"The energy is palpable, people are just excited to see a band that is great."

Another musical act, from Illinois, told the BBC on Thursday it needed to raise $175,000 to cover another night in a hotel, additional food, and bus costs back to the city of Champaign.

"Things are going well due to the very generous support of so many amazing human beings," said Professor Barry Houser, director of the University of Illinois Marching Illini.

By Friday, 3,500 donors had stepped up to help the 410 students and their travel party. "This is truly phenomenal," said Houser.

While awaiting the parade, musicians and punters alike have sheltered from the heavy wind and rain brought by the storm to eastern areas of the US.

Hundreds of thousands of homes were without power in the storm's aftermath Friday, and coastal areas had flooded. The National Weather Service (NWS) expects conditions to improve gradually on Friday.

items.title: Agostini: “Marquez piangeva troppo dopo il Mondiale. Ma ora non potrà battere i miei record”
items.summary: L’ex campione che ha premiato lo spagnolo a Portimao: “È un grande dispiacere, dovevo capirlo su quel palco”
items.content:
Giacomo Agostini ci è rimasto male. «Sarà un grande dispiacere non vedere più Marc Marquez in pista . Quel ragazzo era speciale: regalava gioia a tutti. Ci mancherà».

Sono passati pochi giorni dal decimo titolo sul palco di Portimao : lei che spunta a sorpresa da una porticina, gli batte una mano sulla spalla e consegna il casco dorato.

«E lui che spalanca gli occhi, mi abbraccia, scoppia a piangere. Lacrime sincere: era davvero emozionato. Forse, avrei dovuto capirlo in quel momento».

«Che aveva finito la benzina, dentro di sé. Quando la fatica supera la gioia, non vale più la pena. Vorrei saperne di più, ma lo immagino: il prezzo del dolore era diventato troppo alto . Ha detto basta ai sacrifici. Erano lacrime di felicità e di sofferenza. Ne ha passate di tutti i colori, in questi anni: non si è mai arreso. E questa non è una resa. Perché ci vuol un coraggio da leone, per smettere in un momento così».

«Da numero 1. Quando ce l’hai sulla carena, quel numero, non vorresti lasciarlo per niente al mondo. Non dimenticate anche che Marquez dice addio a un ingaggio milionario, a contratti veramente importanti con gli sponsor. Meriterebbe un altro abbraccio solo per questo. Tempo fa mi aveva detto: “Vado avanti fino a quando potrò lottare per il podio. Altrimenti, smetto”».

Avrà temuto di non essere pronto per la “rivoluzione” del 2027: da 1000 a 850 cc, addio all’aerodinamica e altre diavolerie.

«Secondo me, il prossimo anno si sarebbe trovato a suo agio più di tutti».

«Bezzecchi. Oppure Acosta, Martin. Di Giannantonio sta facendo grandi progressi. Anche Aldeguer ha talento. È impossibile fare previsioni, ma se Marc avesse corso, non avrei avuto dubbi».

L’altro giorno non la finivate più di farvi i complimenti a vicenda.

Qualcuno sostiene che dovrebbe tifare più per l’italiano Valentino, che per Marc lo spagnolo.

«Tifo per lo sport, per il talento. Lo hanno entrambi, sono due campioni che hanno fatto innamorare milioni di tifosi».

E se si avverasse quel suo sogno? La gara davanti a 500mila persone, con Mike Hailwood, Kenny Roberts, Jarno Saarinen, Valentino e Marquez: chi sale sul podio?

«La risposta è scritta sulla pagella. Davanti finisco io, con 15 titoli. Dopo Angel Nieto, mica lo possiamo dimenticare. Il terzo, lo sapete».

Marc Marquez. Che non potrà più insidiarle il record assoluto: allora non è vero, che ci è rimasto male.

«Da questo punto di vista, meglio così ( sorride ). Considerati i miei anni, credo resterò davanti ancora un po’. Facciamo che vedo qualcun altro arrivare a quota 14, però poi si ritira. Siamo onesti: a chi fa piacere essere sorpassato?».

items.title: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter
items.summary: Ukraine settles in for another devastating winter as the questions persists: how will it all end?
items.content:
Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.

I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.

We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.

Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% — way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.

What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.

Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method — sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia — "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a café here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.

It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.

There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.

The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.

So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.

items.title: All'asta l'ultimo sogno degli ingegneri Saab: una berlina da 490 CV mai prodotta in serie
items.summary: Quattro esemplari della NEVS Emily GT, la berlina elettrica sviluppata dagli ex ingegneri Saab, finiscono all'asta insieme all'intero progetto industriale
items.content:
A Trollhättan si chiude un altro capitolo della storia automobilistica svedese. Dopo la vendita delle ultime Saab 9-3 rimaste all'interno dello stabilimento, adesso tocca alla NEVS Emily GT, una berlina elettrica che avrebbe meritato ben altro destino. Sviluppata da una squadra di tecnici nella quale figuravano numerosi ex ingegneri Saab, l'automobile non è mai riuscita a raggiungere la produzione di serie.Dal 25 novembre 2026, sulla piattaforma svedese Klaravik, è possibile partecipare all'asta che riguarda non soltanto gli esemplari costruiti, ma anche tutto ciò che servì per realizzarli. Carrozzerie, componenti, attrezzature e disegni tecnici cercano un nuovo proprietario. Quanto rimane, insomma, di un progetto industriale interrotto quando sembrava avere ancora parecchio da raccontare.

Quattro motori elettrici direttamente nelle ruote

Lo sviluppo della Emily GT cominciò fra il 2019 e il 2020, proprio negli ambienti che avevano ospitato per decenni la produzione delle Saab. Gli ingegneri svedesi scelsero una soluzione meccanica decisamente poco convenzionale, collocando un motore elettrico all'interno di ciascuna ruota. L'idea era quella di superare alcuni dei vincoli progettuali delle tradizionali architetture automobilistiche, sfruttando le possibilità offerte dalla gestione indipendente della coppia sulle quattro ruote.[gallery ids="297543,297542,297541"]La potenza complessiva raggiungeva i 360 kW, equivalenti a circa 490 CV, numeri tutt'altro che trascurabili per una berlina sportiva. Quando venne mostrata pubblicamente nella primavera del 2023, la Emily GT suscitò parecchio interesse, soprattutto per l'originalità delle soluzioni adottate. In fondo, proprio quella propensione a sperimentare aveva caratterizzato le migliori stagioni della Saab. Il progetto, tuttavia, non andò oltre la realizzazione di alcuni prototipi, lasciando senza seguito il lavoro svolto a Trollhättan.

All'asta non soltanto le automobili, ma l'intero progetto

La vendita organizzata da Klaravik comprende quattro esemplari completi, gli unici che, stando agli organizzatori, verranno mai offerti attraverso una vendita pubblica. A questi si aggiunge una quinta automobile, utilizzata come muletto durante lo sviluppo, oltre a carrozzerie, ricambi, accessori e documentazione progettuale.La particolarità dell'asta risiede proprio nella natura del materiale disponibile. Un collezionista potrebbe essere interessato a conservare una delle rarissime Emily GT, mentre per un eventuale acquirente industriale assumerebbero particolare valore i disegni e i componenti utilizzati durante lo sviluppo. possa richiamare l'attenzione degli appassionati Saab di tutto il mondo. Anche per Carita Nero, CEO di Klaravik, si tratta di una vendita fuori dall'ordinario, alla quale è affidato il compito di accompagnare dignitosamente l'uscita della Emily GT dalla sua città natale. Le offerte potranno essere presentate online fino al 9 dicembre 2026.

Anche il robotaxi Sango cerca un nuovo proprietario

Parallelamente alla Emily GT, Klaravik ha messo all'asta un altro progetto sviluppato da NEVS. Si tratta di Pons, presentato nel 2020 e concepito per ripensare il trasporto pubblico urbano attraverso veicoli elettrici a guida autonoma.La sua espressione concreta era il robotaxi Sango, progettato per accogliere fino a sei passeggeri. Particolarmente interessante l'organizzazione dell'abitacolo, che prevedeva la possibilità di separare gli spazi attraverso apposite pareti divisorie, offrendo maggiore riservatezza a chi preferiva viaggiare da solo. Anche in questo caso la vendita comprende l'unico veicolo completo realizzato e il materiale relativo al suo sviluppo.Per Trollhättan sono giorni dal sapore inevitabilmente malinconico. La Emily GT rappresenta l'ultima automobile sviluppata nella città che, per oltre mezzo secolo, aveva legato il proprio nome alla Saab. Difficile sapere se qualcuno raccoglierà davvero il lavoro degli ingegneri scandinavi. Per il momento, ciò che resta di quella promettente berlina elettrica attende un acquirente.

items.title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
items.summary: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks to end the war.
items.content:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.

"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.

Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".

The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced .

Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say

Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend

Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.

Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.

So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".

"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.

The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.

Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."

He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin.

"You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.

Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.

Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.

But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.

"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.

He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.

"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."

Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.

On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.

Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".

He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.

But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.

Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.

Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.

"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

items.title: Oppo inizia a rendere a pagamento i servizi AI: prime segnalazioni in India
items.summary: Tre piani, fino a quasi 10 euro al mese.
items.content:
Pare che ci stiamo lentamente ma inesorabilmente avvicinando alla fase in cui i nodi dell'AI vengono al pettine, e i grandi produttori di smartphone iniziano a decidere che è ora di monetizzare, dopo aver presentato per anni la tecnologia integrata negli smartphone come un vantaggio gratuito. Già da qualche giorno si mormora su Samsung con la sua Galaxy AI, ma Oppo sembra aver saltato del tutto la fase dei rumor, passando direttamente a introdurre la novità. Per ora ci sono riscontri solo in India, ma è lecito assumere che per il resto del mondo sia solo questione di tempo.

Un leaker considerato generalmente piuttosto affidabile ha condiviso degli screenshot apparentemente provenienti da uno smartphone basato su ColorOS 17 in cui l'utente ha la possibilità di scegliere fra tre piani: Basic, Pro e Ultra, rispettivamente al prezzo di 289, 579 e 959 rupie al mese, al cambio pari a circa 2,84, 5,69 e 9,43 euro, che corrispondono a 20.000, 50.000 e 100.000 crediti. Questi crediti costituiscono un pool condiviso tra soprattutto tre funzionalità avanzate: l'interprete vocale in tempo reale, la modifica delle foto tramite comandi vocali con linguaggio naturale e la trascrizione audio.

 You Now Have to PAY to Use AI Features on OPPO Phones! OPPO has introduced subscription-based AI plans for ColorOS, and some of its popular AI features will now require credits to use! Here's how the pricing works in India: - Basic Plan: ₹289/month - 20,000 credits - Pro Plan: ₹579/month - 50,000 credits - Ultra Plan: ₹959/month - 1,00,000 credits These credits are shared across 3 AI features: - Live Translation - AI Photo Agent - Transcription You get approximately: - Basic: 50 Photo Agent uses / 100 mins translation - Pro: 125 Photo Agent uses / 250 mins translation - Ultra: 250 Photo Agent uses / 500 mins translation Top-up credits are also available, starting at ₹189 for 10,000 credits. The good news? Other existing basic AI features will remain FREE. Only these 3 features consume credits. What do you think about OPPO charging a monthly subscription for AI features that come built into your smartphone?

items.title: Mozilla Firefox, la nuova interfaccia Nova sta per diventare obbligatoria
items.summary: Già dal mese prossimo la flag per disabilitarla sarà rimossa, a quanto pare.
items.content:
Vi piace Nova, il nuovo design dell'interfaccia di Firefox introdotta negli scorsi mesi? No? Beh, peggio per voi, a quanto pare Mozilla si prepara a rimuovere la possibilità di disattivarla, rendendola di fatto obbligatoria o inevitabile. La modifica diventerà effettiva a partire già dal mese prossimo: in concreto non sarà più possibile aprire la pagina di impostazioni avanzate (basta dirigersi all'indirizzo about:config) e disabilitare la flag browser.nova.enabled.

Mozilla ha introdotto Nova a inizio 2026 per facilitare la transizione a Firefox per gli utenti che provengono da browser basati su Chromium (sostanzialmente tutti, visto che Chrome, Edge, Opera, perfino Samsung Internet si basano sul codice open-source di Google, debitamente modificato e adattato alle esigenze di ogni produttore). Secondo l'organizzazione, la distribuzione di Nova è ormai completa e mantenere il controllo per disattivarla potrebbe causare comportamenti imprevisti o compromettere il funzionamento del browser.

Del resto sono già passati diversi mesi, come dicevamo, e Mozilla ha avuto modo di limare molte imprecisioni dell'interfaccia, anche tenendo conto dei feedback, delle richieste e delle critiche della community. Per esempio, con Firefox 161 sono arrivati nuovi temi Classic, con colori uniformi e privi di sfumature. C'è anche una variante grigia che richiama l'aspetto della precedente interfaccia Proton. La società ha anche introdotto un comodissimo pulsante Fire nella barra degli strumenti, che permette di cancellare la cronologia con un solo click, e dove l'ha ritenuto opportuno non ha avuto paura di fare un passo indietro, per esempio per l'indicatore laterale delle schede contenitore, che è stato ripristinato nella modalità a schede verticali. Inoltre, Firefox supporta ora completamente la Compact Mode.

items.title: Pop!_OS 26.04 LTS, arrivano desktop remoto e tavolette grafiche
items.summary: Pop!_OS 26.04 LTS è scaricabile. Lupgrade dalla 24.04 sarà attivato a dicembre.
items.content:
Pop!_OS 26.04 LTS è disponibile e porta nel desktop COSMIC il supporto per le tavolette grafiche, il desktop remoto e un modo più rapido per cambiare l'aspetto del sistema. Se avete già Pop!_OS 24.04 LTS, il passaggio da una versione all'altra verrà abilitato a dicembre, mentre hi vuole installare la 26.04 da zero può invece scaricare subito l'immagine dal sito di System76. Alcune delle novità grafiche potrebbero esservi già familiari, perché COSMIC riceve aggiornamenti anche fra una versione della distribuzione e la successiva.

Una delle aggiunte si chiama Constellations. Se cambiate spesso il vostro sfondo e poi passate a sistemare colori, caratteri e icone, ora potete intervenire su tutti questi elementi insieme. Nelle impostazioni di aspetto del desktop scegliete un tema e potete anche ritoccarlo, per esempio aggiungendo un effetto vetro satinato. items.title: Perovskite, una cucitura molecolare fa durare di più le celle solari
items.summary: Una rete di legami fra gli strati rende le celle in perovskite più resistenti e stabili.
items.content:
Una cella solare in perovskite ha raggiunto il 27,04% di efficienza in laboratorio grazie a una rete di minuscoli legami che tengono insieme due dei suoi strati. La prova arriva dall'Università di Scienza e Tecnologia di Hong Kong, che ha pubblicato il lavoro su Nature Photonics. L'efficienza certificata è del 26,67%, ma la cosa da tenere d'occhio, però, è quanto a lungo le celle hanno continuato a lavorare una volta messe sotto carico.

Se guardate com'è fatta una di queste celle, trovate la perovskite che assorbe la luce e, subito accanto, uno strato che raccoglie e trasporta gli elettroni. La giunzione fra i due deve restare ben aderente, perché è da lì che passa parte della corrente. Con il riscaldamento e il raffreddamento durante il funzionamento si accumulano sollecitazioni e possono formarsi crepe, e nella pratica anche materiali capaci di convertire bene la luce perdono resa se si separano proprio nel punto in cui devono scambiarsi le cariche.

Il gruppo di Hong Kong ha messo molecole capaci di unirsi fra loro in entrambi gli strati e poi ha usato il calore per avviare la reazione. Si sono formati legami chimici che attraversano la giunzione e funzionano un po' come i punti di una cucitura. Nei test la resistenza alla propagazione delle crepe è risultata quasi tripla. Ma la'setto particolarmente positivo è che la cucitura lascia anche passare le cariche, così il rinforzo meccanico può convivere con una resa elettrica elevata.

items.title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
items.summary: Paul Mackenzie is found guilty of killing his followers, weeks after being jailed for the mass murder of children.
items.content:
A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.

Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.

Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.

Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.

Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.

The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.

Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.

The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the cases against him.

"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.

The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".

Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.

Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.

The defendants had claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.

assault causing actual bodily harm and five counts of cruelty to a child

being in possession of an article connected with an offence under Kenya's Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2012.

Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders

Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in branches across Kenya.

A television station called Times TV would broadcast his sermons from his church in the resort town of Malindi.

His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".

After the main church shut down in 2019, Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.

The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest.

"We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," said survivor Peter Shukrani, who was rescued after falling ill.

When the shallow graves were discovered, local men were hired for the horrifying task of exhuming the remains.

"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."

"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."

Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".

Post-mortem records showed many of the victims had died of starvation while the remains of others were mostly skeletal, making the establishment of their cause of death impossible.

Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he had lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.

"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court last month.

"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest. I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."

The deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.

The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.

items.content:
Il Citizen Series8 880 GMT nero e dorato è comparso sullo store americano del marchio, ma la buona notizia è che si trova già anche presso rivenditori italiani. Il modello in questione è NB6092-01E, e vanta caratteristiche davvero uniche. Ha un quadrante in carbonio forgiato e il motivo cambia leggermente fra un orologio e l'altro, perché la trama nasce comprimendo fibre di carbonio spezzettate e resina. Può interessarvi? Sappiate che non sarà così facile accaparrarsene uno, perché per la tiratura Citizen indica 1.300 pezzi nella scheda internazionale e in quella europea, mentre lo store statunitense riporta 1.400 esemplari non numerati per la stessa referenza.

La cassa è in acciaio da 41 millimetri, con una parte in tonalità dorata a motivo damascato e una finitura nera che riprende il colore del quadrante. Il cinturino è grigio, in pelle, con una chiusura pieghevole che si apre premendo due pulsanti nascosti. Guardando il quadrante trovate il datario a ore tre e gli indici luminosi sotto il vetro zaffiro, che ha un trattamento antiriflesso per facilitare la lettura in piena luce.

La sigla GMT è quella che vi interessa se viaggiate spesso o lavorate con un paese in un altro fuso, e accanto alle tre lancette tradizionali ce n'è una dedicata a una seconda ora. Potete regolare la lancetta delle ore locali a scatti di un'ora senza toccare le altre indicazioni. E se usate la lunetta girevole delle 24 ore, il calibro automatico 9054 permette di leggere fino a tre fusi.

items.title: Windows, Microsoft vuole prendere il controllo diretto dello sviluppo dei driver
items.summary: La società è convinta che in questo modo il sistema operativo diventerà più affidabile, sicuro e stabile. È un lavorone, ma i primi passi sono già stati compiuti.
items.content:
Microsoft vuole ridurre i problemi di stabilità di Windows intervenendo su una delle loro cause più frequenti: i driver, soprattutto quelli sviluppati da produttori terzi. In occasione della conferenza Ignite 2026, la società ha annunciato un'iniziativa per realizzare direttamente una serie di nuovi driver "di base", in grado di garantire le funzionalità essenziali di un numero più ampio di periferiche senza richiedere l'installazione di componenti aggiuntivi. Microsoft intende applicare questo approccio a intere categorie di dispositivi, partendo da uno dei "nemici" storici più acri dell'intero ecosistema Windows: le stampanti.

Un primo passo in questo senso è già stato compiuto, con Windows Ready Print. Ma la società vuole andare ben oltre, e dice di aver già iniziato i lavori di sviluppo per nuovi driver audio, tra cui quelli per SoundWire e SDCA, destinati a diventare parte integrante del sistema operativo. Sono inoltre in lavorazione driver per bus I3C, adattatori Ethernet USB e fotocamere basate sullo standard MIPI.

Il programma si inserisce nella Driver Quality Initiative (DQI), presentata durante una recente Windows Hardware Engineering Conference. L'iniziativa punta a innalzare gli standard di qualità, sicurezza e affidabilità dei driver, per esempio cercando di tenere il codice non Microsoft il più distante possibile dal kernel di Windows. Tutto questo potrebbe in un certo senso rendere più rigoroso e uniforme l'ecosistema, limitando la possibilità per gli OEM di introdurre funzionalità proprietarie nell'infrastruttura dei driver. Un approccio per certi versi vicino a quello adottato storicamente da Apple.

items.title: Lancia compie 120 anni: la storia di un marchio che ha insegnato all'Italia a innovare
items.summary: Lancia festeggia 120 anni dalla fondazione. Dalle intuizioni di Vincenzo Lancia ai trionfi nei rally, fino al nuovo corso con Ypsilon e Gamma
items.content:
Per molti italiani, Lancia non è mai stata soltanto una marca di automobili. È stata la macchina desiderata da ragazzi, quella ammirata passando davanti alla vetrina di un concessionario, quella che un padre comprava dopo anni di sacrifici. Per altri è stata il rumore di una Stratos nel bosco o l'attesa, al freddo, del passaggio di una Delta Integrale. Ognuno custodisce un frammento diverso della stessa storia.E oggi, 27 novembre 2026, quella storia compie 120 anni. Era il 1906 quando Vincenzo Lancia e Claudio Fogolin fondarono a Torino una Casa automobilistica destinata a lasciare un'impronta profondissima nella cultura industriale italiana. Difficilmente avrebbero potuto immaginare quanto affetto avrebbe suscitato, oltre un secolo dopo, il nome scelto per la loro impresa.

Quando a Torino si costruiva il futuro

Vincenzo Lancia aveva corso con le Fiat, conosceva la meccanica e possedeva quella curiosità che distingue un bravo tecnico da un autentico innovatore. Già la 12 HP del 1908, poi denominata Alpha, adottava un telaio ribassato e una trasmissione a cardano. Nel 1922 la Lambda portò su strada la scocca portante e le sospensioni anteriori indipendenti. Soluzioni che oggi possono apparire scontate, ma che allora richiedevano coraggio progettuale.L'Aprilia, ultima automobile voluta dal fondatore, nacque nel 1936 con una particolare attenzione all'aerodinamica e alle sospensioni indipendenti sulle quattro ruote. Nel 1950 arrivò l'Aurelia, prima vettura di serie al mondo equipaggiata con un motore V6. È forse in questa stagione che va ricercata l'essenza più autentica della Lancia: costruire automobili sofisticate senza necessariamente ostentarne la superiorità tecnica. Una filosofia che, molti anni dopo, avrebbe trovato una declinazione persino nella piccola Y10.

L'Italia più bella, quella raccontata dalle automobili

C'è una scena della nostra cinematografia che vale più di qualsiasi campagna pubblicitaria: Vittorio Gassman al volante dell'Aurelia B24 Convertibile ne Il sorpasso di Dino Risi. Era il 1962 e quell'automobile sembrava fatta apposta per raccontare le contraddizioni, le ambizioni e la voglia di vivere dell'Italia del miracolo economico.L'Aurelia B24 Spider, disegnata da Pininfarina e costruita in soli 240 esemplari, appartiene alla stessa irripetibile stagione creativa. Seguirono le Flaminia, le Flavia, le Fulvia, fino alla Gamma Coupé di Aldo Brovarone e alla Thema 8.32, con quella meravigliosa atmosfera restituita dalla pelle e dalla radica.Poi c'era l'altra Lancia, quella sporca di fango, con i fari supplementari accesi e le carrozzerie segnate dalle pietre. Fulvia, Stratos, 037 e Delta hanno regalato al marchio dieci mondiali Costruttori nei rally. Due anime apparentemente lontanissime, quella sportiva e quella elegante, che hanno saputo convivere sotto lo stesso stemma.

Centoventi anni dopo, una storia ancora da scrivere

Oggi Lancia prova a ritrovare il proprio spazio attraverso Ypsilon e Gamma. La prima conserva - in mezzo alla condivisione con altri brand di Stellantis - qualche prezioso riferimento stilistico al passato, dai fanali circolari della Stratos alle forme morbide delle grandi Lancia di un tempo, interpretando la mobilità contemporanea con motorizzazioni termiche, ibride ed elettriche.La nuova Gamma, disegnata a Torino e costruita a Melfi, segna invece il ritorno del marchio fra le grandi viaggiatrici. Lunga 4,67 metri, nasce sulla piattaforma STLA Medium e propone una versione ibrida da 145 CV, elettriche con autonomia fino a 740 chilometri e una HF Integrale da 375 CV.Rivedere a Milano AutoClassica la Gamma del 1976 accanto alla sua erede è stato un incontro dal significato particolare. Perché Lancia possiede un patrimonio che nessuna operazione di marketing potrebbe ricreare dal nulla: la memoria affettiva di intere generazioni. Adesso deve meritarsi quella delle prossime. Ed è forse questo l'augurio più bello che possiamo farle nel giorno del suo centoventesimo compleanno.[drivek_widget brand_id="lancia" model_id="ypsilon-elettrica"]
